source_text: Καὶ οὕτω γίνεται κύκλος καὶ χορὸς ἐναρμόνιος, συμφωνούντων πάντων καὶ συστοιχούντων ἀλλήλοις. Ὅθεν κυρίως αὐτοῖς καὶ ἡ προσηγορία τῶν στοιχείων ἐφήρμοσται. Ταῦτά μοι εἴρηται παριστῶντι τὴν αἰτίαν δι' ἣν ὁ Θεὸς τὴν ξηρὰν ἐκάλεσε γῆν, ἀλλ' οὐχὶ τὴν γῆν προσεῖπε ξηράν. Διότι τὸ ξηρὸν οὐχὶ τῶν ὕστερον προσγινομένων ἐστὶ τῇ γῇ, ἀλλὰ τῶν ἐξ ἀρχῆς συμπληρούντων αὐτῆς τὴν οὐσίαν. Τὰ δὲ αὐτὴν τοῦ εἶναι αἰτίαν παρέχοντα, πρότερα τῇ φύσει τῶν μετὰ ταῦτα προσγινομένων καὶ προτιμότερα. Ὥστε εἰκότως ἐκ τῶν προϋπαρχόντων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων ἐπενοήθη τῇ γῇ τὰ γνωρίσματα. 4.6 Καὶ εἶδεν ὁ Θεὸς ὅτι καλόν. Οὐκ αὐτὸ τοῦτο τερπνήν τινα ὄψιν θαλάσσης ὁ λόγος ἐνδείκνυται τῷ Θεῷ πεφηνέναι. Οὐ γὰρ ὀφθαλμοῖς βλέπει τὰ κάλλη τῆς κτίσεως ὁ ποιητὴς, ἀλλὰ τῇ ἀρρήτῳ σοφίᾳ θεωρεῖ τὰ γινόμενα. Ἡδὺ μὲν γὰρ θέαμα, λευκαινομένη θάλασσα, γαλήνης αὐτὴν σταθερᾶς κατεχούσης· ἡδὺ δὲ καὶ ὅταν πραείαις αὔραις τραχυνομένη τὰ νῶτα, πορφύρουσαν χρόαν ἢ κυανῆν τοῖς ὁρῶσι προσβάλλῃ· ὅτε οὐδὲ τύπτει βιαίως τὴν γείτονα χέρσον, ἀλλ' οἷον εἰρηνικαῖς τισιν αὐτὴν περιπλοκαῖς κατασπάζεται. Οὐ μὴν οὕτω καὶ Θεῷ οἴεσθαι χρὴ τὴν Γραφὴν εἰρηκέναι καλὴν καὶ ἡδεῖαν ὦφθαι τὴν θάλασσαν, ἀλλὰ τὸ καλὸν ἐκεῖ τῷ λόγῳ τῆς δημιουργίας κρίνεται. Πρῶτον μὲν, ὅτι πηγὴ τῆς περὶ γῆν ἁπάσης νοτίδος ἐστὶ τὸ τῆς θαλάσσης ὕδωρ· τοῦτο μὲν ἐν τοῖς ἀφανέσι πόροις διαδιδόμενον, ὡς δηλοῦσιν αἱ σομφώδεις τῶν ἠπείρων καὶ ὕπαντροι, ὑφ' ἃς ἡ ῥοώδης διαυλωνίζουσα θάλασσα, ἐπειδὰν σκολιαῖς καὶ οὐ πρὸς τὸ ὄρθιον φερομέναις ἐναποληφθῇ διεξόδοις, ὑπὸ τοῦ κινοῦν τος αὐτὴν πνεύματος ὠθουμένη, φέρεται ἔξω τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν διαρρήξασα, καὶ γίνεται πότιμος ἐκ τῆς διηθήσεως τὸ πικρὸν ἰαθεῖσα. Ἤδη δὲ καὶ θερμοτέρας ἐκ μετάλλων ποιότητος κατὰ τὴν διέξοδον προσλαβοῦσα, ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς τοῦ κινοῦντος αἰτίας ζέουσα γίνεται, ὡς τὰ πολλὰ, καὶ πυρώδης· ὅπερ πολλαχοῦ μὲν τῶν νήσων, πολλαχοῦ δὲ τῶν παραλίων τόπων ἔξεστιν ἱστορῆσαι. Ὅπου γε καὶ κατὰ τὴν μεσόγειαν, τόποι τινὲς τῶν ποταμίων ὑδάτων γείτονες, ὡς μικρὰ μεγάλοις εἰκάσαι, τὰ παραπλήσια πάσχουσι. Πρὸς οὖν τί τοῦτο εἴρηταί μοι; Ὅτι πᾶσα ὑπόνομός ἐστιν ἡ γῆ, διὰ πόρων ἀφανῶν ἐκ τῶν ἀρχῶν τῆς θαλάσσης ὑπονοστοῦντος τοῦ ὕδατος. 4.7 Καλὴ τοίνυν ἡ θάλασσα τῷ Θεῷ, καὶ διὰ τὴν ἐν τῷ βάθει τῆς ἰκμάδος ὑποδρομήν· καλὴ καὶ διότι ποταμῶν οὖσα δοχεῖον, εἰς ἑαυτὴν τὰ πανταχόθεν καταδέχεται ῥεύματα, καὶ μένει τῶν ὅρων εἴσω τῶν ἑαυτῆς· καλὴ καὶ διότι τοῖς ἀερίοις ὕδασιν ἀρχὴ τίς ἐστι καὶ πηγὴ, θαλπομένη μὲν τῇ ἀκτῖνι τοῦ ἡλίου, ἀποτιθεμένη δὲ τὸ λεπτὸν τοῦ ὕδατος διὰ τῶν ἀτμῶν, ὅπερ ἑλκυσθὲν εἰς τὸν ἄνω τόπον, εἶτα καταψυχθὲν διὰ τὸ ὑψηλότερον γενέσθαι τῆς ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐδάφους ἀνακλάσεως τῶν ἀκτίνων, καὶ ὁμοῦ τῆς ἐκ τοῦ νέφους σκιᾶς τὴν ψύξιν ἐπιτεινούσης, ὑετὸς γίνεται, καὶ πιαίνει τὴν γῆν. Καὶ τούτοις οὐδεὶς ἀπιστεῖ πάντως τοὺς ὑποκαιομένους λέβητας ἐννοήσας, οἳ πλήρεις ὄντες ὑγροῦ, πολλάκις κενοὶ κατελείφθησαν, εἰς ἀτμὸν παντὸς τοῦ ἑψομένου διακρι θέντος.
thought_title: The circle of elements and the goodness of the sea
orientation: Basil is explaining why God called the dry land 'earth' rather than calling the earth 'dry,' and now turns to the meaning of 'And God saw that it was good' regarding the gathered waters.
pass_a_gloss: And so there comes to be a circle and a harmonious dance, all things agreeing and standing in order with one another. Whence properly the name of elements has been fitted to them. These things have been said by me presenting the reason through which God called the dry land earth, but did not address the earth as dry. Because the dry is not of the things that come to be added later to the earth, but of the things that from the beginning fill up its substance. And the things that provide to it the cause of being are prior in nature to the things added after these and more honorable. So that reasonably from the things pre-existing and older the distinguishing marks were devised for the earth. 4.6 And God saw that it was good. The word does not indicate that this very thing, some pleasant sight of the sea, appeared to God. For the maker does not see the beauties of the creation with eyes, but with ineffable wisdom he beholds the things that come to be. For it is a sweet spectacle, the sea growing white, when a steady calm holds it; and sweet also when, roughened on its back by gentle breezes, it casts a purple or dark-blue color upon those who see; when it does not strike violently the neighboring dry land, but as if with certain peaceful embraces it kisses it. Not however thus must one think that the Scripture has said that the sea appeared beautiful and sweet to God, but the good there is judged by the word of the creation. First, because the water of the sea is a source of all moisture around the earth; this being distributed in the unseen passages, as the porous and hollow places of the continents show, under which the flowing sea passing through channels, whenever it is caught in crooked passages not leading straight upward, being pushed by the spirit that moves it, is carried outside having broken through the surface, and becomes drinkable, having healed its bitterness through the filtering. And already also having taken on a hotter quality from metals along the passage, from the same cause of the moving thing it becomes boiling, for the most part, and fiery; which thing it is possible to observe in many places of the islands, and in many places of the coastal regions. Where indeed also in the interior, certain places neighboring the river waters, to compare small things with great, suffer similar things. To what purpose then has this been said by me? That all the earth is underground-mined, the water stealing away from the sources of the sea through unseen pores. 4.7 Beautiful therefore is the sea to God, also because of the under-running of moisture in the depth; beautiful also because, being a receptacle of rivers, it receives into itself the streams from everywhere, and remains within its own boundaries; beautiful also because to the aerial waters it is a certain beginning and source, being warmed by the ray of the sun, and putting off the fine part of the water through the vapors, which having been drawn up to the upper region, then having been cooled because it came to be higher than the reflection of the rays from the ground, and at the same time the shadow from the cloud intensifying the cooling, becomes rain, and fattens the earth. And no one disbelieves these things at all, having considered the heated cauldrons, which being full of liquid, often were left empty, all of the boiled thing having been separated into vapor.

choices.why: Preserves the musical and choral metaphor Basil uses for the ordered interrelation of the elements.
Keeps the sense of constitutive completion from the beginning, not later addition.
Renders the identifying characteristics derived from pre-existing qualities.
Preserves the vivid personification of the sea's gentle contact with the land.
Conveys the image of the earth being threaded with hidden channels, matching Basil's point about unseen water passages.
rejected: the earth is full of underground passages

choices.why: Captures the motion of moisture running beneath the surface, a key part of Basil's hydrological explanation.

bible_refs.note: καὶ εἶδεν ὁ Θεὸς ὅτι καλόν

pass_b_english: And so a circle and a harmonious dance comes into being, with all things in agreement and standing in order with one another. This is why the name “elements” is properly fitted to them. I have said all this to show the reason God called the dry land “earth,” but did not call the earth “dry land.” For dryness is not one of the things added to the earth later; it is one of the things that fill up its substance from the beginning. And the things that give it its cause of being are prior by nature and more honorable than the things added afterward. So it was reasonable that the earth’s distinguishing marks were conceived from what pre-existed and was older.

“And God saw that it was good” (Genesis 1:10). The text does not mean that some pleasant sight of the sea appeared to God. For the Maker does not see the beauties of creation with eyes, but contemplates what comes into being with ineffable wisdom. A whitening sea is a sweet sight when a steady calm holds it; it is sweet too when its back is roughened by gentle breezes and it casts a purple or dark-blue color before those who watch—when it does not strike the neighboring land violently, but kisses it as if with peaceful embraces. But we must not think Scripture means that the sea appeared beautiful and sweet to God in this way. Rather, the good there is judged by the reasoning of the Creator's work.

First, the water of the sea is the source of all moisture around the earth. It is distributed through hidden channels, as the porous and cavernous places of the continents show. Beneath them the flowing sea runs in channels, and when it is caught in winding passages that do not run straight, it is pushed by the spirit that moves it, breaks through the surface, and flows outside—and becomes drinkable, its bitterness healed by the filtering. Sometimes it also takes on a hotter quality from metals along the way, and from the same cause that moves it, it often becomes boiling and fiery. This can be observed in many islands and many coastal places. Even inland, some places near river waters—to compare small things with great—suffer something similar. Why have I said this? Because all the earth is undermined, with water making its way beneath from the sources of the sea through hidden pores.

So the sea is good to God also because of the under-running of moisture in its depths. It is good also because it is the reservoir of rivers, receiving streams from everywhere into itself, and yet remains within its own boundaries. It is good also because it is a beginning and source for the waters in the air: it is warmed by the sun’s ray and sends off the fine part of the water through vapors. This is drawn up to the upper region, then cooled because it has risen higher than the reflection of the rays from the ground—and at the same time the shade from the cloud intensifies the cooling—and it becomes rain and enriches the earth. No one doubts these things who has considered heated cauldrons: full of liquid, they are often left empty when everything being boiled has been dispersed into vapor.

problems.why: ὑπόνομος means 'undermined/tunneled under', not 'mined' in the modern extractive sense.

fixed: Changed 'underground-mined' to 'undermined': the source ὑπόνομός ἐστιν ἡ γῆ means the earth is tunneled under or undermined, not mined in the extractive sense.

problems.why: λόγῳ here means 'account' or 'reasoning', not 'principle'; refers to rational explanation.
problems.fix: by the reasoning of the Creator's work

edits.old: Rather, the good there is judged by the principle of creation.
edits.new: Rather, the good there is judged by the reasoning of the Creator's work.

fixed: Changed 'the principle of creation' to 'the reasoning of the Creator's work' because λόγῳ here means 'account' or 'reasoning', not 'principle'.

last_rejected.quote: the things that give it its cause of being
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὰ δὲ αὐτὴν τοῦ εἶναι αἰτίαν παρέχοντα
last_rejected.why: Greek says 'the things providing the cause of its existence,' not 'give it its cause of being.'
last_rejected.fix: the things that provide the cause of its existence
last_rejected.ruling: 'Cause of being' and 'cause of its existence' are equivalent; no meaning changed.

last_rejected.quote: the earth's distinguishing marks were conceived
last_rejected.why: Greek passive: 'the distinguishing marks were devised/assigned to earth,' not earth conceived them.
last_rejected.fix: the distinguishing marks were assigned to earth
last_rejected.ruling: Passive 'were conceived' preserves Greek passive; no agent wrongly introduced.

last_rejected.quote: the reasoning of the Creator's work
last_rejected.why: λόγος here means 'principle' or 'rational plan,' not 'reasoning' as a process.
last_rejected.fix: the principle of the Creator's work
last_rejected.ruling: 'Reasoning' is within λόγος range; meaning not substantially changed.

last_rejected.why: πνεῦμα here likely means wind/air pressure, not 'Spirit'; context is physical explanation.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Spirit' is valid for πνεῦμα; context clarifies physical force, not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: from the same cause that moves it
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐκ τῆς αὐτῆς τοῦ κινοῦντος αἰτίας
last_rejected.why: Same issue: 'the thing that moves it' (wind/pressure), not abstract 'cause that moves it.'
last_rejected.fix: from the same thing that drives it
last_rejected.ruling: 'Cause that moves it' adequately renders αἰτίας; no meaning lost.

last_rejected.quote: the under-running of moisture in its depths
last_rejected.source_quote: τὴν ἐν τῷ βάθει τῆς ἰκμάδος ὑποδρομήν
last_rejected.why: ὑποδρομή means 'secret flow/run beneath,' not 'under-running in depths'; moisture runs beneath earth.
last_rejected.fix: the secret flow of moisture beneath
last_rejected.ruling: 'Under-running in depths' captures ὑποδρομή + βάθει adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἀέριος means 'in the air' as location, but 'waters of the air' or 'atmospheric waters' is clearer.
last_rejected.ruling: 'Waters in the air' correctly renders ἀερίοις ὕδασιν; mere preference only.
